title: Computational method for the identification of third generation activity cliffs
author: Stumpfe, Hu, et al.
materials: 3.2. As potency difference criterion for AC formation, the value of the mean of the distribution plus two standard deviations (sigma) is used.

steps.title: Select target sets
steps.instruction: Pre‑select target sets whose compound potency distributions have an interquartile range (IQR) of at least one order of magnitude (IQR ≥ 1), because such sets are more likely to contain activity cliffs.

steps.title: Identify activity substructures (iAS)
steps.instruction: For each compound in the selected target sets, apply the compound‑core relationship (CCR) methodology: fragment exocyclic single bonds according to RECAP rules, allowing a maximum of five fragmentation sites per compound; each fragmentation yields a core and a substituent. Retain only fragments where the core contains at least twice the number of non‑hydrogen atoms of the substituent (or combined substituents). Replace each substituent at a site with a hydrogen atom to obtain a generalized core representation. Group all compounds that share the same core into an activity substructure (AS).

steps.title: Enumerate analog pairs within AS
steps.instruction: For every AS, enumerate all possible analog pairs (compounds sharing the same core) and compute the potency difference for each pair. These analog pairs, whether differing at a single substitution site or multiple sites, serve as the similarity criterion for activity‑cliff (AC) formation.

steps.title: Collect potency differences
steps.instruction: Gather all analog‑pair potency differences from all ASs belonging to a given target set and determine the statistical distribution of these differences.

steps.title: Define potency‑difference threshold
steps.instruction: Calculate the mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) of the potency‑difference distribution for the target set; set the AC formation threshold to μ + 2 σ.

steps.title: Identify third‑generation ACs
steps.instruction: Select all analog pairs (single‑site and multi‑site) whose potency difference exceeds the threshold (μ + 2 σ); these constitute the third‑generation activity cliffs.

steps.title: Characterize multi‑site ACs
steps.instruction: For each multi‑site AC, use the OpenEye chemistry toolkit to search for single‑site analogs that contain each individual substitution. This enables assessment of the contribution of each substitution to the overall potency change.
